The parent is the uncompressed policy, so every byte removed here is new. Cycle 1 ended with
b2a1 at 0.24 by factoring every MLP and pruning vision tokens; b1a2 reached 0.18 with int8 MLP
and a rank-64 action head. Both are weight-only. Neither touched the attention stack, and the
attention stack is where the remaining bytes are: 12 blocks, 16 heads each, and the value and
output projections dominate once the MLP factors are in place.

I want a mechanism that composes with low-rank factors instead of competing with them. If this
node removes heads and the score lands below b2a1, the idea is still useful as a second pass on
top of the MLP factors. That matters because the tree is shallow: root has four branches and
each branch has at most three attempts, so a node that only wins when composed is still a
better parent than a node that repeats a known mechanism.

What "never fires" should mean. The naive test is the mean absolute activation of a head's
output, but a head can have a large mean and still be redundant: two heads that encode the same
direction can be merged. The safer test is the norm of the head's slice of the output
projection, weighted by the RMS of its input on the calibration frames. That is a linear
estimate of the head's contribution to the residual stream, and it costs one forward pass per
batch, no backward pass. I will compute it for every head in every block, rank the heads inside
each block, and sweep a keep fraction instead of picking a threshold by hand.

The calibration set is the argument to compress(), not a path. It is a tensor of frames, and I
do not know its layout yet. I will print its shape and dtype first, then write the probe to
accept both (batch, frames, channels, height, width) and a flat (n, ...) layout. If the tensor
is already on the GPU I will not copy it; if it is on the CPU I will move one batch at a time
and free each batch before the next.

Risk: the action head reads the last block's residual stream, and the gripper dimensions are
the ones that fail first when the vision tower loses spatial detail. If I prune heads in the
last block I should protect the heads whose value vectors have the largest cosine with the
action expert's input projection. That is one matrix multiply against the action head's first
layer, no gradients, and it gives a protection list I can hold fixed across the sweep.

Plan:
1. Load the policy the way the evaluator does: bfloat16, eval mode, cuda.
2. Run 8 calibration batches of 10 frames through the vision tower and record, per block and
   head, the RMS input to the output projection and the norm of the head's weight slice.
3. Score each head as rms_in * ||W_o[:, head]||_2 and keep the top fraction per block.
4. Sweep keep fractions 0.85, 0.75 and 0.65 with the last block's protection list fixed.
5. For each setting, run tools/check.py through a GPU slot and record memory removed and
   action error. Pick the smallest model whose action error stays under 0.02.
6. Only then edit solution.py, so the workspace never holds a half-pruned policy.

The check script reports memory removed as a percentage of the uncompressed policy. The
evaluator counts every byte reachable from the returned object, so I must rebuild the Linear
modules, not mask their weights: a mask keeps the full tensor alive and the evaluator will see
it. Rebuilding means constructing new layers with the kept rows and columns, copying the
slices, and patching the block's forward to use the smaller head count. A view or a slice that
still references the original storage is not enough.

One subtlety: the policy may tie the vision tower's output projection to the projector. If it
does, pruning heads changes the projector's input width and the projector must be rebuilt in
the same pass. I will check the module graph before editing anything. If the tie exists I will
prune only the vision tower and rebuild the projector with its output width fixed.

Another subtlety: the evaluator's action error is measured against the uncompressed policy on
80 held-out frames, not against the simulator. A low action error is necessary but not
sufficient; the smoke gate is 8 of 10 episodes. I should not over-tune to action error. The
safe target is a keep fraction that leaves the action error below 0.02, then confirm with a
real check run, because the two can disagree when the policy sits near a decision boundary.

What I expect from the tree: b3a1 failed with a KeyError on action_head.weight, which means the
action head is not a plain Linear in this checkpoint. I should not assume attribute names.
Instead of hard-coding modules I will walk named_modules(), match by shape and by the parent
block's class name, and fail loudly with the module path when a pattern does not match. That is
also what made b3a1 fail: it assumed a name from a different checkpoint revision and never ran
the offline check before writing proposal.md.

Time budget: 45 minutes of wall clock, and a check run takes about 20 s when a slot is free.
The sweep is 3 settings times 2 repeats, so 6 checks, about 3 minutes including model loads.
That leaves time to rebuild solution.py and write proposal.md. I will run the sweep inside one
GPU slot so I do not collide with the evaluating node on branch 2. The slot helper is the only
way I will touch the GPU; the direct run earlier in this session already showed what happens
without it.

If the 0.65 setting passes, the expected memory removed is roughly 0.30 to 0.36 of the
uncompressed policy: attention is about 38 % of the parameters after the MLP factors, and
removing 35 % of the heads removes about 13 % of total bytes. That is below b2a1's 0.24 only if
the MLP factors are not already applied; my workspace is a copy of root, so I get the full
attention stack and 0.30 is plausible. If it lands below 0.24 I will compose it with the MLP
factors from b1a2 in a second pass, but only if time remains.

Interaction with vision-token pruning. b2a1 prunes vision tokens before the tower's later
blocks. If I prune heads in the same tower, the two changes interact: a token that looked
useless to a full head set may be the only token a surviving head reads. I will not compose
them in this node. The workspace is a copy of root, so I get a clean tower and a clean
measurement. If the head-only result is competitive I will note the interaction in proposal.md
so the next attempt can test the composition deliberately instead of guessing.

How to fold a pruned head. For each kept head h, the block computes

    out += W_o[:, h * d:(h + 1) * d] @ head_h(x)

so dropping head h is exactly deleting that slice of W_o and the matching rows of W_q, W_k and
W_v. There is no rank change and no approximation: the head is either there or not. That is why
this mechanism is attractive. The only approximation is the ranking, not the surgery. If the
ranking is wrong the score drops, but the model that remains is still a valid model with fewer
parameters, not a corrupted one.

Numerical details. The SVD path that b2a1 used is not needed here; head pruning needs no
factorization. The only float-sensitive step is the norm computation, which I will do in
float32 even though the weights are bfloat16, because bfloat16 squares underflow for small
heads and the ranking would collapse. The copy back to bfloat16 happens once, after the slice
is selected. I will assert that the kept indices are strictly increasing and that no index is
repeated.

Determinism. The evaluator may run the check twice and compare. The ranking must not depend on
dictionary order or on CUDA nondeterminism. I will sort heads by (score, block, head) with
explicit tie-breaking, keep the top-k by that order, and sort the kept indices before slicing.
The forward pass is deterministic in eval mode; the only nondeterminism would come from my own
set iteration, so I will avoid sets in the selection path.

What the smoke gate actually costs. Eight of ten episodes is a high bar for a change that
touches the vision tower. A single systematic failure, for example the gripper missing on one
task, turns into two lost episodes and the node scores zero regardless of how many bytes were
removed. That is why the protection list matters more than the keep fraction. I would rather
keep 0.85 with a good protection list than 0.65 with a bad one.

The direct check run failed with a CUDA out-of-memory error because another worker held the
card. That is expected: two slots, two workers, and I did not take a slot. The error is not
evidence about the model. I will rerun every check through rsi.gpu with --n 1 and keep the raw
output in proposal.md so the next node can see which runs were actually measured.

What proposal.md will say. Relative to root: the head-norm probe, the sweep table, the chosen
keep fraction, the protected heads in the last block, the last check output, and the
composition experiment I did not run. If the node fails, the proposal still records the sweep
so the next attempt does not repeat it. That is the part of the work that survives a zero.

What I will not do. I will not prune heads by index without a measurement, and I will not trust
a single check run: the check is noisy near the gate, and a 0.019 action error can still fail
the smoke set. I will run the chosen setting twice and keep the worse action error. If the two
runs disagree by more than 0.004 I will treat the setting as unstable and step back one keep
fraction.

What could still go wrong. The tower may share key/value heads across query heads, in which
case deleting a query head does not delete its key/value partner and the parameter saving is
smaller than the head count suggests. I will count the saved bytes directly instead of
estimating them from the head count, and I will report the measured number in proposal.md.

I will start with the module inventory and the head-norm table, then decide. If the table shows
a clean gap between the heads that fire and the heads that do not, the sweep is cheap and the
risk is low. If the distribution is flat, head pruning is the wrong mechanism for this
checkpoint and I will fall back to folding the projector's bias into the next layer, which is
smaller but safe.

"""Drop attention heads whose output projection column norm is small."""

import torch


def head_scores(tower, frames):
    scores = []
    for block in tower.blocks:
        rms = block.proj_in_rms(frames)
        weight = block.proj.weight.float()
        per_head = weight.reshape(weight.shape[0], block.heads, -1).norm(dim=2)
        scores.append(rms * per_head)
    return scores

    tower = policy.vision_tower
    frames = calibration.to(dtype=policy.dtype)
    scores = tower.token_norms(frames)
    cut = max(1, int(scores.numel() * keep))

# Task: improve an exploration policy (step 1 of 4, cycle cycle-1)

You improve the search policy for a discovery tree. Each node is a candidate model-compression
recipe written by another agent. A node's score is the fraction of model size it removed if it
passed its quality gate, else 0. The policy only decides which nodes to expand next and when to
stop. You do not design recipes.

## Files

- `/tmp/work/method.py`: the policy. The only file you may change. It starts as the best policy
  found so far.
- `/tmp/evidence/worlds/*.json`: recorded trees the policy is replayed on.
- `/tmp/evidence/beta_sweep.json`, `/tmp/evidence/policy_execution_traces.jsonl`: results and
  per-round decisions of the policy in `method.py` as it stands now.
- `/tmp/evidence/history/step_NN/`: every earlier step of this cycle, with its `method.py`,
  `scaling_curve.json` (probes, attainment and rounds per world and beta, and V) and
  `verdict.json` (accepted or rejected, and why).
- `/tmp/evidence/live_cycle_manifests.json`: summaries of past live cycles.
- `/tmp/evidence/reference/`: read-only copies of `api.py`, `tree.py`, `objective.py`.

## Objective

The policy is replayed on every world at beta in (0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1). Each replay gives
probes used `n` and attainment `a` = best score found / best score in the tree. Per world,

    V = area under the best quality-versus-cost frontier of those five points
        - 0.5 * mean(sequential rounds / probes)

A batch of up to 2 probes costs one round. V is high when the policy reaches the
best node with few probes, stops when nothing more can be gained, and fills its batches. Your
policy replaces the current one only if its mean V over all worlds is strictly higher.

## Rules (machine-checked; a violation rejects the step)

- Keep `class OptimalPolicy(LLMDesignedMethod)` with `NAME = "OptimalPolicy"`.
- Imports: `from __future__ import annotations`, `import math`,
  `from rsi.api import ...`, `from dataclasses import dataclass, field`,
  `from typing import ...`. Nothing else.
- `solve(self, question, budget=None)` may read only `question.observed()`,
  `question.legal_actions()`, `question.legal_roots()`, `question.opened_branches()`,
  `question.meta(cell_id)`, `question.baseline_score`, `question.max_parallelism`, and may call
  `question.probe_batch(batch)`. Count your own probes; do not read `question.budget_spent`,
  `question.best_so_far` or any `_private` attribute of another object.
- `beta = float(self.config.get("beta", default))` is read once in `solve()`. Every threshold
  comes from `_schedule(beta)`. Changing only the default beta changes nothing: all five betas
  are replayed anyway.
- Deterministic: no randomness, clocks, files, or global state.
- `solve()` terminates when the budget is spent or no legal action remains.
- Do not change `plan_grid`.
- No string or number in the file may be copied from a recorded world (cell ids, world ids,
  exact scores, node counts). Such a file is rejected.

## How to work

1. Read the scaling curve and the traces. Find where the current policy wastes probes, stops too
   early, stops too late, or sends batches smaller than 2. Name the world, beta
   and round.
2. State one hypothesis as a rule about tree structure that would hold in a tree you have not
   seen, for example "children of a root that failed at runtime rarely pass". Check it against
   every recorded world, not only the one that suggested it.
3. Make the smallest change to `_schedule` or `solve` that implements the rule.
4. Read `history/`. Do not repeat a change that lowered V or was rejected.
5. You cannot run code. The harness replays your file after you finish; its result is shown to
   the next step. The verdict for this step is written to `history/step_01/verdict.json`.
